question: The Greek Government is asking for the ‘national escape clause’ to be extended to include corporate groups involved in energy infrastructure projects. The aim is to promote EUR 1.5 billion in investments for the three-year period from 2026 to 2028, which means more fast cash for corporate groups, stolen from the people's coffers.

While energy corporations in Greece made a record profit of EUR 2 billion in 2025, households have been seeing a steady increase in electricity prices since 2021. In view of the above, where does the Commission stand on the following: 1.

The fact that the ‘escape clause’ will free up more large sums of money from Member States’ coffers in order to incentivise investments in big energy corporations, with the people having to foot the bill at a time when they are struggling under the yoke of high prices?

The fact that the EU’s energy policy consists of support and funding measures such as ‘pass’ subsidies – aimed at securing profits for energy corporations (also known as ‘green birds of prey’) and energy infrastructure giants –, which essentially perpetuate the high prices borne by ordinary people and secure profits for big corporate groups?

The fact that the energy policy of the EU and the national governments is sending energy prices and poverty rates through the roof, while ordinary people are subjected to decrepit and unsafe infrastructure in an ancient network where corporate groups only promote investment if they are able to secure conditions that will maximise their profit, meaning that the people will continue to foot the hefty bill multiple times over?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The war in the Middle East and its impact on the European energy system call for exceptional action to strengthen the system’s structural resilience and security.

The aim of broadening the National Escape Clause for defence to energy security measures is to allow Member States to request extra flexibility for handling significant upfront costs to ensure Europe's long-term energy security. The scope and the eligibility criteria for the flexibility require any measure benefiting from it to make a direct contribution to accelerating the energy transition.
To ensure continued fiscal sustainability, the scale of the overall flexibility is capped and integrated into the existing framework for fiscal surveillance.

A wide range of measures are eligible: support for households and businesses to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels and promote decarbonisation, measures that accelerate the electrification of end-use sectors, support for investment in electricity grids, clean energy storage (e.g. batteries), energy saving and the capacity expansion of clean energy sources.

Member States can also consider the broader range of measures included in the AccelerateEU Communication1 and the Electrification Action Plan2, aligned with the eligibility criteria outlined in the Guidance Note adopted on 18 August 20263. Member States benefiting from the additional flexibility will need to provide sufficient evidence that the measures adopted on this basis are eligible.
This will be assessed by the Commission on a case-by-case basis.

1 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/accelerateeu-strengthen-eu-energy-resilience_en. 2 https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/eus-energy-system/electrification_en. 3 See Commission Notice on Guidance to Member States on Broadening the Scope of the National Escape
